sources_inspected_in_original_images.document: Comments on the AUTODIN II Phase I Technical Specification and a Set of Recommendations (draft), prepared by R. E. Kahn for an ad hoc DCA technical advisory committee

pages.content: Committee convened at DCA request, members served individually; did not consider whether to proceed; met 26-27 August 1975 at the Reston facility of the DCEC; briefed by Dr. Lebow, Colonel Stathopoules, Dr. Helm; findings presented afternoon 27 August and to General Paschall the following morning; findings unanimously agreed; membership in Appendix A; five determinations listed.
Unanimous recommendation that the RFP with the current technical specification not be publicly released without major revisions.

Five areas of comment; recommendation 1 on specifying the deliverable by performance criteria; quoted example requiring a standard communications protocol that allows but does not require host and switch co-location.

Recommendations 3 and 4: management split after IOC and a technical split between backbone and subscriber access equipment; access equipment includes TAC and host access devices that may provide sequencing for hosts that cannot conform.

Recommendations 5 and 6: contractor operational control of the backbone, DCA operational control of subscriber access equipment; contractor transit-time and throughput responsibility limited to the backbone because performance evaluation should not depend on host protocol implementations and customer provided equipment. The contrast clause on specifiability crosses a skewed line break and is paraphrased, not quoted.

1 second transit time called excessive and unnecessary, 0.1 second sought for an average 500-bit packet; restricting contractor responsibility to the backbone makes transit-time and throughput requirements independent of host systems; recommendations 8 and 9 on loose coupling, uniform interfaces, and avoiding a monolithic non-decomposable switch.
Recommendations 10 to 13: backbone insensitive to host protocol change, DCA certification of host access equipment, a reference implementation, and a separately contracted front end.

Separation of TAC and packet switch including for encryption reasons; link encryption as an interim measure with end-to-end encryption and a PLI test; isolation of security-relevant software into small modules.

Recommendation 22, verbatim: the committee strongly recommends that the requirement for sequencing be eliminated from the backbone packet switching network; in lieu of this, sequencing shall be provided by a front-end computer, the users' mainframe computer or by a Host access mechanism. Rewrite goals: robustness and reliability, ability to interconnect with other packet networks, capability for possible introduction of end/end encryption.

Specific change recommended is to move the sequencing function out of the backbone and into the front-end mainframe or TAC; deadlock-free source-to-destination flow control giving precedence to priority traffic without depending on sequencing or logical connections; logical-link function is properly a host function; closing sentence that required subnet priority mechanisms demand out-of-sequence delivery. A contemporary reader's handwritten marginal note reading WHAT? I DON'T UNDERSTAND THIS circles the sentence about logical links duplicating the Host to Host protocol; the hand is not identified.

Paragraph b ties host-level sequencing to interconnection, fragmentation for different maximum packet sizes, and end-to-end encryption, and asks for source-to-destination flow control independent of sequencing and a plan compatible with computers on different packet switching networks communicating via standard host protocols. Paragraph c: host/packet-switch interface to be specified in detail by DCA, compatible with end-to-end security and gateway interconnections, another network treated as a particular type of Host connection; maximum packet lifetime, transmission thresholds, non-blocking normal mode.
Gateways recommended instead of overlapping Satin IV header and AUTODIN II leader.

Committee membership: R. E. Kahn (ARPA, Chairman), V. G. Cerf (Stanford University), M. Pirtle (NASA/Ames), J. Postel (Stanford Research Institute), J. Markowitz (Central Intelligence Agency), D. Wood (Mitre Corporation), A. Vezza (Massachusetts Institute of Technology). Earlier OCR read the heading as APPENDIX 4; the original reads APPENDIX A.

pages_inspected_in_original.content: Identity, dates, contract, page count, and the abstract's revises-and-replaces statement.

Adaptive routing and retransmissions may cause out-of-order arrivals; segments of differing precedence from multiple sources make the SCM-to-SIP stream multiplexed and unordered; no guarantees against duplication, loss, or nonsequenced delivery; recovering lost segments, resequencing, demultiplexing, and end-to-end accountability are the responsibilities of the end users or any higher level protocol acting on their behalf; Non-Delivery Notices; window flow control.

General BSL field descriptions. TCP Version Number identifies the originating SIP's user, is ignored by the network, and is used by the destination SIP to pass the segment to the proper higher level protocol. Source and destination subscriber addresses are the SIP's single logical address, associated with the SIP and its access line.
Data segment to SCM processing; precedence ceiling on the access line with validation reject; start of the TCP Version No. field description.

pages_read_from_extracted_text_only.content: Formal specification after extensive redesign since the original System Performance Specification; SIP is how TAC, SCCU and MCCU access components communicate with the backbone and a host may use it directly; pure packet transport service; the protocol is not burdened with connection and sequencing functions.

Background specification list: AUTODIN II System Performance Specification (type WAN) Nov 1975 as amended through September 1976 plus approved Specification Change Notices; System Design (Technical) Specification from the Western Union proposal part 5, April 76, refinements June and August 76, best and final offer October 76; AUTODIN II Final Design Plan June 1978; AUTODIN II Design Executive Summary 18 May 1978.

Layered architecture of link and segment protocols; only the host SIP interpreter's stimuli and responses are specified, and those are what will be tested and certified before a subscriber host may operate on the network; internal SIP interfaces are host unique and unspecified.
Figure 2-5, Levels of Precedence: four user categories with subcategories over four bits; CAT I-1 and I-2 network only; I-3 CRITIC/ECP; I-4 FLASH and others.
TCP Version Number continuation: the code for the AUTODIN II TCP is one, the code for no TCP is zero, all other codes are reserved and will be assigned by DCA Code 530.

conclusions.within_autodin_ii: Established at both ends, undetermined in between. An August 1975 committee unanimously recommended removing the backbone sequencing requirement and named front-end, mainframe, or host access mechanism as the alternatives, arguing partly from priority. The specification in force in March 1979 assigns resequencing to end users or a higher level protocol and names precedence among its causes. No decision record is held, and independent arrival from ARPANET experience remains open.
conclusions.influence_on_research_tcp_ip: Strengthened as setting, contradicted as stated motive. Cerf and Postel served on the committee, and its page 12 links host-level sequencing to interconnection, fragmentation across different packet sizes, and end-to-end encryption. IEN 2 nonetheless argues the split from layering with no mention of AUTODIN, precedence, priority, or security.
